headline: Records give way to yield-driven wobble as bubble talk grows
body: The tape has been of two minds this week. The S&P 500 closed above 7,800 for the first time on Tuesday and the Nasdaq Composite notched its own fresh record alongside it, extending a rally that AI and chip names have led for months. That strength cracked by midweek as the 10-year Treasury yield surged to roughly 5.3-5.4%, its highest level since 2002, on sticky inflation data (an ISM services prices-paid reading at its highest since mid-2022) and a modest repricing toward the odds of another Fed hike rather than the cuts markets had been leaning on. The S&P and Nasdaq each slipped only modestly on the pullback, but small caps took the bigger hit, with the Russell 2000 down over 1% -- a sign the damage concentrated away from the mega-cap names still propping up the headline indices.

Underneath the record closes, breadth looks thinner than the index levels suggest, and that's drawing more scrutiny than usual: commentary this week leaned on comparisons between today's AI-driven concentration in the top names and prior bubble peaks, and survey data has shown a notable jump in money managers naming an AI-equity bubble as the market's top tail risk versus a month ago. Retail and social-media chatter didn't turn up anything concrete enough to cite today -- searches for WallStreetBets and Stocktwits trending activity surfaced no clear, current reads -- so this take leans on price action, yields, and positioning commentary rather than invented social-sentiment specifics. Net effect: a market still at records, but one where the bond market and concentration concerns are doing more to set the mood than broad-based conviction.
